entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: The speaker or the evidence *implies* (suggests something without saying it); the listener *infers* (draws a conclusion from it).
entries.usage: Use *imply* for the person or data that sends the hidden message and *infer* for the person who works it out. Many natives say *infer* for *imply* in speech, but editors and careful writers treat that as an error.
examples: Are you **implying** that I didn't do my share?
From his tone, I **inferred** that he was unhappy with the plan.
The results **imply** a strong seasonal effect.

drill.sentence: From her manager's two-word reply, she {{inferred}} that he was annoyed.
drill.hint: imply or infer? (she is the one drawing the conclusion)

mistake.wrong: What are you inferring?
mistake.right: What are you implying?
mistake.why: The speaker implies; the listener infers.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Effective* means something produces the result you want; *efficient* means it produces that result without wasting time, money or energy.
entries.usage: Something can be effective but inefficient (it works, but slowly or at high cost) or efficient but ineffective (fast and cheap, but it does not work). In research and business writing, choose by what you mean: success or economy. In medicine, *efficacy* is how well a treatment works in trials and *effectiveness* how well it works in real life.
examples: The new drug is highly **effective**, but it costs $80,000 per patient.
The new pipeline is far more **efficient**: the same job now runs in half the time.
Heat pumps are much more **efficient** than space heaters, so your electric bill goes down.

drill.sentence: The ad campaign was cheap and quick to run, but it wasn't {{effective}}: sales didn't go up at all.
drill.hint: effective or efficient? (the question is whether it worked)

mistake.wrong: This method is very effective: it uses half the memory.
mistake.right: This method is very efficient: it uses half the memory.
mistake.why: Saving resources is efficiency; *effective* only says that something works.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *I.e.* (Latin *id est*) means *that is* and restates or narrows what you just said; *e.g.* (*exempli gratia*) means *for example* and introduces one or more examples.
entries.usage: Test it by reading it aloud: if *that is* or *in other words* fits, use *i.e.*; if *for example* fits, use *e.g.* Do not end an *e.g.* list with *etc.*, since *e.g.* already shows that the list is incomplete. American style puts a comma after both (*e.g.,*), and they belong mainly in parentheses, notes and technical writing.
examples: We only used public datasets (**e.g.**, ImageNet and COCO), so anyone can reproduce our results.
Please submit all receipts by the end of the fiscal year (**i.e.**, June 30).
Sign up with your school email (**i.e.**, the one ending in .edu) to get the student discount.

drill.sentence: Pack a few layers ({{e.g.}}, a fleece and a rain jacket), since the weather in the mountains changes fast.
drill.hint: i.e. or e.g.? (these are only some of the possible layers)

mistake.wrong: Bring a snack (i.e., fruit or granola bars).
mistake.right: Bring a snack (e.g., fruit or granola bars).
mistake.why: Fruit and granola bars are only examples of snacks; *i.e.* would mean nothing else counts.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: Use *fewer* with plural count nouns (*fewer people*, *fewer errors*) and *less* with mass nouns (*less time*, *less noise*).
entries.usage: Careful writers and editors follow this rule, although *less* with plurals is common in casual speech and on supermarket signs (*10 items or less*). Amounts of time, money, distance and percentages take *less* even when plural (*less than 10 miles*, *less than $50*), because you think of them as one quantity.
examples: Our new car uses **less** gas and needs **fewer** repairs than the old one.
There were **fewer** than 20 people at the talk, so it felt more like a seminar.
The drive took **less** than three hours, even with traffic.

drill.sentence: With the new filter, I'm getting far {{fewer}} spam emails than last month.
drill.hint: fewer or less? (emails can be counted)

mistake.wrong: There were less people at the conference this year.
mistake.right: There were fewer people at the conference this year.
mistake.why: *People* is a plural count noun, so careful English uses *fewer*.

entries.label: confusable words
entries.meaning: *Ensure* means make certain that something happens; *insure* means protect with an insurance policy; *assure* means tell a person something to remove their doubt.
entries.usage: *Assure* takes a person as its object (*I assure you*), while *ensure* takes the result (*ensure that the data is backed up*). In American English *insure* is also accepted for *make certain*, but most editors keep it for insurance. A simple rule for formal writing: people are assured, results are ensured, property is insured.
examples: We fixed the random seed to **ensure** that every run is reproducible.
Most people **insure** their homes against fire but not against floods.
The pilot **assured** the passengers that the turbulence was nothing to worry about.

drill.sentence: Before the demo, I {{assured}} the client that the system had been fully tested.
drill.hint: ensure, insure or assure? (removing a person's doubt)

mistake.wrong: I ensure you that everything will be ready by Friday.
mistake.right: I assure you that everything will be ready by Friday.
mistake.why: To remove someone's doubt, use *assure* + person; *ensure* takes a result, not a person.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Complement* (with *e*) means complete something or go well with it; *compliment* (with *i*) means praise, or a remark of praise.
entries.usage: The two words sound exactly the same, so the mistake happens only in writing. A memory aid: a *complement* completes something, and a *compliment* is something *I* like to get. *Complimentary* also means free (*complimentary breakfast*), while *complementary* means fitting together (*complementary skills*).
examples: The two postdocs **complement** each other: one is strong in theory, the other in experiments.
My neighbor **complimented** me on my garden, which made my whole week.
A dry white wine will **complement** the fish nicely.

drill.sentence: Thanks — that's the nicest {{compliment}} anyone has paid me since I started teaching.
drill.hint: complement or compliment? (a remark of praise)

mistake.wrong: Thanks for the complement on my talk!
mistake.right: Thanks for the compliment on my talk!
mistake.why: Praise is spelled with *i*; *complement* means something that completes or goes well with another thing.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Systematic* means done methodically, step by step, according to a plan; *systemic* means affecting or built into a whole system rather than one part.
entries.usage: *Systematic* is usually positive (*a systematic review*, *systematic testing*), although in science a *systematic error* is a consistent bias in measurement. *Systemic* is common in policy, medicine and finance: *systemic racism*, *systemic risk*, *a systemic infection*. Ask whether you mean a method (*systematic*) or a whole system (*systemic*).
examples: She's very **systematic** about packing: she makes a list and checks off every item.
The 2008 crisis showed how one bank's failure can create **systemic** risk for the whole economy.
Unlike a local skin infection, a **systemic** infection spreads through the bloodstream.

drill.sentence: The report argues that the delays aren't one manager's fault but a {{systemic}} problem across the agency.
drill.hint: systematic or systemic? (built into the whole organization)

mistake.wrong: We conducted a systemic review of the literature.
mistake.right: We conducted a systematic review of the literature.
mistake.why: A review done by a fixed method is *systematic*; *systemic* means affecting a whole system.

entries.label: confusable words
entries.meaning: *Peak* is the highest point, or to reach it; *peek* is a quick, often secret look; *pique* means arouse, almost always in *pique someone's interest* or *curiosity*.
entries.usage: All three are pronounced the same, so *peaked my interest* and *a sneak peak* are common written errors, even among native speakers. The fixed forms are *piqued my interest*, *a sneak peek*, *peak hours* and *at its peak*. As a noun, *pique* also means irritation (*in a fit of pique*).
examples: The odd title **piqued** my interest, so I picked up the book.
Here's a sneak **peek** at the new interface before we launch it next week.
Flu cases usually **peak** in January or February.

drill.sentence: The "Do Not Open" sign on the box only {{piqued}} the kids' curiosity.
drill.hint: peak, peek or pique? (aroused a feeling)

mistake.wrong: The trailer really peaked my interest.
mistake.right: The trailer really piqued my interest.
mistake.why: To arouse interest is *pique*; *peak* means reach the highest point.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Affect* means influence or change something; the much rarer verb *effect* means bring about or cause to happen, as in *effect change*.
entries.usage: As verbs, *affect* is the everyday word (*the delay affected everyone*), while *effect* is formal and appears mainly in *effect change* or *effect a transfer*. The difference matters: to *affect* a policy is to influence it, but to *effect* a policy is to put it in place. In fast speech they sound almost the same, so the error is mostly in writing.
examples: The new parking fees will **affect** everyone who drives to work downtown.
She joined the board hoping to **effect** real change in how the company treats its workers.
Lack of sleep **affects** memory more than most people realize.

drill.sentence: It took the new director two years to {{effect}} any real change in the department's culture.
drill.hint: affect or effect? (bring about, cause to happen)

mistake.wrong: The budget cuts will effect every department.
mistake.right: The budget cuts will affect every department.
mistake.why: To influence something is *affect*; the verb *effect* means bring about, which makes no sense here.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: The whole *comprises* the parts (*the team comprises five people*); the parts *compose* the whole, and the whole *is composed of* the parts.
entries.usage: *Is comprised of* is very common, even in good newspapers, but many editors and style guides still mark it as wrong; *consists of* or *is composed of* is always safe. In formal writing, use *comprise* without *of*. In everyday speech, *is made up of* is the natural choice.
examples: The committee **comprises** four faculty members and two students.
The dataset **is composed of** 12,000 chest X-rays from three hospitals.
Women now **compose** more than half of the students in American medical schools.

drill.sentence: The full survey {{comprises}} 40 questions, divided into four sections.
drill.hint: comprise or compose? (the whole is the subject, and no *of* follows)

mistake.wrong: The United States is comprised of 50 states.
mistake.right: The United States comprises 50 states.
mistake.why: Strict usage says the whole *comprises* its parts, with no *of*; *is comprised of* is common, but many editors correct it.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Principal* is an adjective meaning main or most important, and a noun for the head of a school or the original sum of a loan; *principle* is only a noun: a basic rule, law or belief.
entries.usage: The two sound identical, so the mistake happens only in writing. A memory aid: a *principle* is a rule (both end in *-le*), and the school *principal* is your *pal*. Fixed phrases with *principle* include *in principle* (in theory), *on principle* (because of your beliefs) and *a matter of principle*.
examples: The **principal** called my parents after I skipped class twice.
She turned down the money as a matter of **principle**.
Rising rents are the **principal** reason young families leave the city.

drill.sentence: I agree with the plan in {{principle}}, but I'm worried about what it'll cost.
drill.hint: principal or principle? (part of a fixed phrase meaning *in theory*)

mistake.wrong: The principle reason for the delay was the weather.
mistake.right: The principal reason for the delay was the weather.
mistake.why: The adjective meaning *main* is *principal*; *principle* is only a noun.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Discreet* means careful not to attract attention or reveal private things; *discrete* means separate and distinct, existing as individual parts.
entries.usage: Both are usually pronounced dih-SKREET (*discrete* is sometimes stressed DIS-kreet), so the mistake is mostly in writing. *Discreet* describes people and behavior (*be discreet*, *a discreet word*, noun *discretion*); *discrete* describes units, steps and categories and is common in math and technical writing (*discrete steps*, *a discrete variable*). A memory aid: in *discrete*, the *t* keeps the two *e*s apart.
examples: Please be **discreet**; nobody at work knows I'm pregnant yet.
The course is divided into six **discrete** modules, so you can take them in any order.
The hotel staff were wonderfully **discreet** about their famous guest.

drill.sentence: The thief wasn't very {{discreet}}: he posted photos of the stolen jewelry online.
drill.hint: discreet or discrete? (careful not to attract attention)

mistake.wrong: Don't worry, I'll be discrete.
mistake.right: Don't worry, I'll be discreet.
mistake.why: Keeping something private is *discreet*; *discrete* means separate.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Continual* means happening again and again, with breaks in between; *continuous* means going on without any break at all.
entries.usage: Careful writers use *continual* for repeated events, often annoying ones (*continual complaints*), and *continuous* for an unbroken flow (*continuous rain*). In everyday writing the two overlap, and *continual* is also used for something that seems never to stop. In technical terms only *continuous* is used: *continuous function*, *continuous monitoring*, *continuous integration*.
examples: The **continual** interruptions from my phone make it impossible to read.
After surgery, the patient was under **continuous** monitoring for 48 hours.
Three days of **continuous** rain flooded our basement.

drill.sentence: The {{continual}} arguments about chores, almost every evening, wore the whole family down.
drill.hint: continual or continuous? (repeated, with breaks in between)

mistake.wrong: A fridge needs a continual supply of power.
mistake.right: A fridge needs a continuous supply of power.
mistake.why: Power that must never stop is *continuous*; *continual* suggests that it keeps stopping and starting.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Economic* means relating to the economy, trade or money in general; *economical* means saving money or resources, not wasteful.
entries.usage: Use *economic* for the economy as a whole (*economic growth*, *an economic crisis*, *economic policy*) and *economical* for things that save money, fuel or space (*an economical car*, *an economical use of space*). *Economical* can also describe concise writing. *Economical with the truth* is an ironic, originally British way to say that someone is hiding facts or lying.
examples: The country took years to recover from the **economic** crisis of 2008.
Buying rice in bulk is much more **economical** than buying small bags.
Her writing is wonderfully **economical**: not a single word is wasted.

drill.sentence: We chose the smaller car because it's more {{economical}} to run.
drill.hint: economic or economical? (cheap to operate)

mistake.wrong: A heat pump is a very economic way to heat your home.
mistake.right: A heat pump is a very economical way to heat your home.
mistake.why: Saving money is *economical*; *economic* is about the economy.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Historic* means important or famous in history, likely to be remembered; *historical* means relating to the past or to the study of history.
entries.usage: A *historic* building or day matters; a *historical* novel, record or figure simply belongs to the past. News uses *historic* for events that will be remembered (*a historic win*, *a historic agreement*). American style is *a historic*, not *an historic*.
examples: Winning the World Cup was a **historic** moment for the whole country.
The library has a large collection of **historical** maps of New England.
The movie is a **historical** drama set during the California Gold Rush.

drill.sentence: Saturday's vote to merge the two towns was {{historic}}: the first change to the county map in 150 years.
drill.hint: historic or historical? (important, will be remembered)

mistake.wrong: Today is a historical day for our club.
mistake.right: Today is a historic day for our club.
mistake.why: An important day that will be remembered is *historic*; *historical* only means about the past.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Alternate* means every other one (*alternate weekends*) or, in American English, a substitute (*an alternate route*); *alternative* means another possible choice.
entries.usage: In American English the adjectives overlap for a substitute option (*an alternate* or *alternative route*); British English uses only *alternative* there. Only *alternate* means *every other* and works as a verb (*alternate between*); only *alternative* is used for a real choice (*no alternative*, *alternative medicine*). As a noun, *an alternate* is a substitute person, such as a jury alternate.
examples: My ex and I have the kids on **alternate** weekends.
If the bridge is closed, take the **alternate** route along the river.
We had no **alternative** but to cancel the trip.

drill.sentence: My son's soccer games are on {{alternate}} Saturdays, so we're free every other week.
drill.hint: alternate or alternative? (every second one)

mistake.wrong: We meet on alternative Mondays.
mistake.right: We meet on alternate Mondays.
mistake.why: *Every other one* is *alternate*; *alternative* only means another option.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Accurate* means close to the true or correct value; *precise* means exact and detailed, or, in measurement, giving nearly the same result every time.
entries.usage: In science and engineering the difference is strict: a scale that always reads two pounds too heavy is precise but not accurate. In everyday speech they overlap, but *precise* stresses exactness and detail (*precise instructions*, *at that precise moment*), while *accurate* stresses being correct (*an accurate description*). In machine learning, *precision* is also the name of a specific metric.
examples: The weather forecast was surprisingly **accurate**: it started raining right at 3 p.m.
At that **precise** moment, the lights went out.
His darts all landed in a tight group just left of the bullseye: **precise**, but not **accurate**.

drill.sentence: My bathroom scale is {{accurate}}: it matches the scale at the doctor's office to within a pound.
drill.hint: accurate or precise? (close to the true value)

mistake.wrong: The scale is accurate: it always shows exactly two pounds too much.
mistake.right: The scale is precise but not accurate: it always shows two pounds too much.
mistake.why: Giving the same result every time is precision; being close to the true value is accuracy.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: A *percentage point* is the simple difference between two percentages; *percent* describes a change relative to the starting value. From 10% to 12% is a rise of 2 percentage points, or 20 percent.
entries.usage: News, finance and research writing need this distinction: *rates rose half a percentage point*. Writing *rose 2%* for a move from 10% to 12% is ambiguous or wrong, and it can make a change sound much smaller or larger than it is. In speech, *points* alone is a common short form (*unemployment fell two points*).
examples: The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter of a **percentage point**.
Unemployment fell from 5% to 4%, a drop of one **percentage point** but 20 **percent** in relative terms.
Our rent went up 8 **percent** this year, from $2,000 to $2,160 a month.

drill.sentence: My bank's savings rate went from 3% to 4%, an increase of one {{percentage point}}.
drill.hint: percent or percentage point? (the simple difference between two rates)

mistake.wrong: The rate rose from 10% to 12%, an increase of 2 percent.
mistake.right: The rate rose from 10% to 12%, an increase of 2 percentage points.
mistake.why: Subtracting one percentage from another gives percentage points; *percent* is the change relative to the starting value.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Random* means happening by chance, with no pattern or plan; *arbitrary* means chosen by someone's whim or without a good reason, often unfairly.
entries.usage: A lottery draw is random; a rule a manager invents on a whim is arbitrary. *Arbitrary* is usually a criticism (*an arbitrary decision*, *the cutoff seems arbitrary*), except in math, where *an arbitrary number* means any one you choose. In casual speech *random* also means odd or unexpected (*some random guy*), which is a different sense.
examples: The winners are chosen at **random** from everyone who entered.
The 5 p.m. deadline seems **arbitrary**; why not 6?
We surveyed a **random** sample of 500 households to avoid bias.

drill.sentence: The coach benched him for no clear reason, and the whole team felt the decision was {{arbitrary}}.
drill.hint: random or arbitrary? (made on a whim, without good reason)

mistake.wrong: We chose an arbitrary sample by drawing names from a hat.
mistake.right: We chose a random sample by drawing names from a hat.
mistake.why: Drawing names leaves the choice to chance, which is *random*; *arbitrary* implies a person's whim.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Ambiguous* describes words, situations or results that can be understood in more than one way; *ambivalent* describes a person who has mixed or conflicting feelings about something.
entries.usage: Things are ambiguous; people and their attitudes are ambivalent (*ambivalent about* or *toward* something). *Ambivalent* is often misused to mean *indifferent*, but it means feeling two opposite ways at once, not feeling nothing.
examples: Her text was **ambiguous**: I couldn't tell if she was joking or annoyed.
I'm **ambivalent** about moving to Denver; I love the mountains, but I'd miss my friends.
The test results were **ambiguous**, so the doctor ordered another scan.

drill.sentence: She's {{ambivalent}} about having kids: part of her wants them, and part of her doesn't.
drill.hint: ambiguous or ambivalent? (a person with mixed feelings)

mistake.wrong: The wording of the contract is ambivalent.
mistake.right: The wording of the contract is ambiguous.
mistake.why: Text with two possible meanings is *ambiguous*; *ambivalent* describes mixed feelings.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Adverse* means harmful or unfavorable (*adverse effects*, *adverse weather*); *averse* means strongly disliking or opposed to something and describes people (*averse to risk*).
entries.usage: *Adverse* goes with effects, conditions, events and reactions; *averse* follows a person and *be*, takes *to*, or forms compounds such as *risk-averse* and *conflict-averse*. *Not averse to* is a common understatement for *quite happy to*. The nouns are *adversity* and *aversion*.
examples: The drug can have **adverse** effects in people with kidney problems.
I'm not **averse** to a little overtime, as long as it's paid.
My parents are very **risk-averse**, so they keep most of their savings in the bank.

drill.sentence: Flights out of Denver were delayed because of {{adverse}} weather over the Rockies.
drill.hint: adverse or averse? (harmful, unfavorable)

mistake.wrong: She is adverse to taking risks.
mistake.right: She is averse to taking risks.
mistake.why: People are *averse* (opposed) to things; *adverse* describes harmful conditions or effects.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Flaunt* means show something off proudly so that others notice; *flout* means openly ignore or break a rule, law or custom.
entries.usage: *Flaunt* takes things you are proud of (*wealth*, *a new car*, *your body*); *flout* takes rules, laws and conventions. *Flaunt the rules* is a very common error, even in print; some dictionaries now record it, but editors and careful writers still treat it as a mistake.
examples: He likes to **flaunt** his new watch at every family dinner.
Drivers who **flout** the speed limit near schools will now face double fines.
My aunt always says, "If you've got it, **flaunt** it."

drill.sentence: Several bars continued to {{flout}} the city's noise rules, playing loud music past 2 a.m.
drill.hint: flaunt or flout? (openly break a rule)

mistake.wrong: Some players flaunt the rules and get away with it.
mistake.right: Some players flout the rules and get away with it.
mistake.why: Breaking rules openly is *flout*; *flaunt* means show off.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Eminent* means famous and respected, especially within a profession; *imminent* means about to happen very soon, usually something bad.
entries.usage: Typical partners are *an eminent surgeon*, *historian* or *scientist* vs. *imminent danger*, *an imminent storm*, *an imminent collapse*. They differ only in the first vowel, EM-uh-nunt vs. IM-uh-nunt, so they are mixed up in speech as well as in writing. *Eminent domain* is the American legal term for the government's right to take private land for public use, with payment.
examples: The talk was given by an **eminent** surgeon who had pioneered the procedure.
Forecasters say landfall is **imminent**, and residents should leave now.
The store's closure is **imminent**; everything's 70% off.

drill.sentence: Dark clouds and sudden gusts of wind told us that a storm was {{imminent}}.
drill.hint: eminent or imminent? (about to happen)

mistake.wrong: She is an imminent scholar of Roman history.
mistake.right: She is an eminent scholar of Roman history.
mistake.why: A respected expert is *eminent*; *imminent* means about to happen.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Elicit* is a verb: to draw out a response, reaction or piece of information from someone; *illicit* is an adjective meaning illegal or forbidden by social rules.
entries.usage: Because they are different parts of speech, the grammar of the sentence shows which one you need: *elicit a response*, *a laugh*, *a confession* vs. *illicit drugs*, *an illicit affair*. They sound almost the same (ih-LIS-it), so the confusion is mainly in writing.
examples: His joke **elicited** only a few polite laughs.
Police found **illicit** drugs hidden in the car's spare tire.
The teacher asked open questions to **elicit** ideas from the quieter students.

drill.sentence: The tabloid was sued for publishing photos of the actor's {{illicit}} affair.
drill.hint: elicit or illicit? (forbidden, not socially allowed)

mistake.wrong: The question illicited a strong reaction from the audience.
mistake.right: The question elicited a strong reaction from the audience.
mistake.why: The verb meaning *draw out* is *elicit*; *illicit* is an adjective meaning illegal.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Lay* takes an object: you lay something down (past *laid*); *lie* means recline and takes no object (past *lay*, past participle *lain*).
entries.usage: The trap is that *lay* is also the past tense of *lie*: *Yesterday I lay in bed* is correct. In casual American speech *lay* for *lie* (*I'm going to lay down*) is very common, but editors and careful speakers still treat it as an error. A quick test for the present tense: if the verb has an object (*lay it down*), use *lay*.
examples: Always **lay** a baby on its back to sleep.
I'm exhausted; I need to **lie** down for an hour.
Yesterday I **lay** in bed until noon, reading.

drill.sentence: The dog likes to {{lie}} in the sun on the back porch all afternoon.
drill.hint: lay or lie? (recline; no object)

mistake.wrong: I'm going to lay down for a few minutes.
mistake.right: I'm going to lie down for a few minutes.
mistake.why: *Lie* (recline) takes no object; *lay* needs one, as in *lay the book down*.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Farther* is used for physical distance; *further* is used for degree, extent or time, and also means *additional* (*further questions*).
entries.usage: Careful American usage keeps *farther* for distance (*a mile farther*) and *further* for figurative extent (*further from the truth*), but *further* for distance is also common and accepted. Only *further* means *additional* and works as a verb (*further your career*). British English mostly uses *further* for both.
examples: The campsite was two miles **farther** than the map suggested.
For **further** information, call the number on the back of your card.
Nothing could be **further** from the truth.

drill.sentence: Thank you, Your Honor, we have no {{further}} questions for this witness.
drill.hint: farther or further? (additional)

mistake.wrong: We need farther discussion before we decide.
mistake.right: We need further discussion before we decide.
mistake.why: Only *further* means *additional*; *farther* is for physical distance.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Definite* means clear, fixed and certain (*a definite answer*); *definitive* means final and authoritative, settling a question, or the best and most complete version (*the definitive biography*).
entries.usage: A *definite* answer is clear; a *definitive* answer comes from a source that settles the question for good. Using *definitive* just to sound stronger than *definite* (*a definitive improvement*) is a common error. Typical partners are *a definite date*, *improvement*, *maybe* vs. *the definitive guide*, *study*, *version*, *ruling*.
examples: We don't have a **definite** date yet, but it'll probably be in June.
Her book is still the **definitive** guide to regional Italian cooking.
There's been a **definite** improvement in his mood since he changed jobs.

drill.sentence: Critics agree that this 1960s recording is the {{definitive}} version of the symphony.
drill.hint: definite or definitive? (the best and most authoritative)

mistake.wrong: The new version is a definitive improvement over the old one.
mistake.right: The new version is a definite improvement over the old one.
mistake.why: An improvement you can clearly see is *definite*; *definitive* means final or authoritative.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Precede* means come or go before something in time, order or position; *proceed* means go forward, continue, or begin an action.
entries.usage: *Precede* takes a direct object (*a dinner preceded the ceremony*); *proceed* takes no object and is usually followed by *with* or *to* (*proceed with the plan*, *proceed to gate 12*). The spellings also differ (*-cede* vs. *-ceed*), and in fast speech the two words sound alike.
examples: A short speech by the mayor **preceded** the fireworks.
Passengers on Flight 214 should **proceed** to gate 12.
The weeks **preceding** the wedding were total chaos.

drill.sentence: After the fire alarm stopped, the teacher told us to {{proceed}} with the exam.
drill.hint: precede or proceed? (continue)

mistake.wrong: Lightning always proceeds thunder.
mistake.right: Lightning always precedes thunder.
mistake.why: To come before is *precede*; *proceed* means go forward or continue.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Evoke* means bring a feeling, memory or image into someone's mind; *invoke* means call on a law, right, principle or authority to support or justify something.
entries.usage: Smells, music and pictures *evoke* things (*evoke memories*, *nostalgia*, *the 1950s*); people *invoke* rules and authorities (*invoke a clause*, *invoke the Fifth Amendment*). In programming, *invoke* also means call a function. *Invoke memories* is a common slip.
examples: The smell of pine always **evokes** summers at my grandparents' cabin.
The mayor **invoked** emergency powers to close the bridge during the flood.
The airline **invoked** a bad-weather clause to avoid paying compensation.

drill.sentence: Those old black-and-white photos {{evoked}} a strong sense of nostalgia in my father.
drill.hint: evoke or invoke? (brought a feeling to mind)

mistake.wrong: The song invokes memories of my first year in New York.
mistake.right: The song evokes memories of my first year in New York.
mistake.why: Bringing memories to mind is *evoke*; *invoke* means call on a rule or authority.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Disparate* means very different from each other, so hard to compare or combine; *desperate* means feeling hopeless, or needing something very urgently.
entries.usage: *Disparate* is formal and usually describes plural nouns: *disparate groups*, *sources*, *ideas*, *data*. *Desperate* is an everyday word: *desperate for a coffee*, *a desperate situation*. The two sound similar, so writers sometimes type *desperate groups* when they mean groups that have little in common.
examples: The team brings together people from **disparate** backgrounds: a nurse, a chef and a former pilot.
After three hours in the car, the kids were **desperate** for a bathroom.
The festival draws **disparate** crowds, from teenage punk fans to retired couples.

drill.sentence: The book tries to connect three {{disparate}} stories, and it never quite works.
drill.hint: disparate or desperate? (very different from each other)

mistake.wrong: The report combines desperate sources of information.
mistake.right: The report combines disparate sources of information.
mistake.why: Sources that differ from each other are *disparate*; *desperate* means hopeless or in urgent need.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: A *precedent* is an earlier action or decision used as an example or rule for later cases; *precedence* is priority, the right to come first.
entries.usage: The fixed phrases are *set a precedent*, *without precedent* and *legal precedent* vs. *take precedence over* and *give precedence to*. The plural *precedents* sounds exactly like *precedence*, so the error is mainly in writing. The adjective *unprecedented* (never seen before) comes from *precedent*.
examples: If we let one student retake the exam, we'll set a **precedent**.
Safety takes **precedence** over speed on this job site.
The court's ruling had no **precedent** in the state's history.

drill.sentence: At our house, homework takes {{precedence}} over video games.
drill.hint: precedent or precedence? (priority)

mistake.wrong: Family always takes precedent over work.
mistake.right: Family always takes precedence over work.
mistake.why: Priority is *precedence*; a *precedent* is an earlier example that guides later cases.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Respectfully* means in a way that shows respect; *respectively* means *in the order just mentioned* and links two lists item by item.
entries.usage: *Respectively* usually comes at the end of a sentence with two matching lists: *Ana and Ben are 7 and 9, respectively*. *Respectfully* describes manner (*listen respectfully*) and introduces polite disagreement (*I respectfully disagree*). Writing *respectively* when you mean *respectfully*, for example in an email sign-off, is a common slip.
examples: I **respectfully** disagree with the board's decision, and I'd like to explain why.
Jake and Sam are 8 and 12, **respectively**.
The kids listened **respectfully** while their grandfather told the same old story again.

drill.sentence: The two finalists, Maria and Tom, scored 92 and 87 points, {{respectively}}.
drill.hint: respectfully or respectively? (in the order just mentioned)

mistake.wrong: Respectively, I don't think that's a good idea.
mistake.right: Respectfully, I don't think that's a good idea.
mistake.why: To soften disagreement, use *respectfully* (with respect); *respectively* only matches items in two lists.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Exacerbate* means make a problem or bad situation worse; *exasperate* means annoy or frustrate a person intensely.
entries.usage: Problems, symptoms and tensions are exacerbated; people are exasperated (*an exasperated sigh*, *exasperated by the delays*). Both are stressed on the second syllable (ig-ZAS-er-bayt, ig-ZAS-puh-rayt), which is one reason they get mixed up. A quick test: if the object is a person, you need *exasperate*.
examples: Scratching will only **exacerbate** the rash.
My dad gets **exasperated** when I lose my keys for the third time in a day.
Closing two lanes for repairs has **exacerbated** traffic on the bridge.

drill.sentence: After explaining the rules for the fifth time, the teacher let out an {{exasperated}} sigh.
drill.hint: exacerbated or exasperated? (frustrated and annoyed)

mistake.wrong: Skipping meals will only exasperate your headache.
mistake.right: Skipping meals will only exacerbate your headache.
mistake.why: Making a problem worse is *exacerbate*; *exasperate* means annoy a person.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Defuse* means make a tense or dangerous situation calmer, or literally remove the fuse from a bomb; *diffuse* means spread out over a wide area, or, as an adjective, spread out and not concentrated.
entries.usage: *Diffuse the situation* is a frequent error in print; careful writers use *defuse* for tension, anger and conflict. *Diffuse* is for light, gas, heat, smells and responsibility (*diffuse light*, *diffuse responsibility*). The pronunciations differ slightly: dee-FYOOZ for *defuse*, dih-FYOOZ for the verb *diffuse* and dih-FYOOS for the adjective.
examples: She **defused** the tension at dinner with a joke about the dry turkey.
A linen lampshade **diffuses** the light so it isn't so harsh.
The smell of fresh coffee slowly **diffused** through the whole apartment.

drill.sentence: The manager stepped in to {{defuse}} the shouting match between two customers.
drill.hint: defuse or diffuse? (calm a tense situation)

mistake.wrong: The teacher tried to diffuse the situation.
mistake.right: The teacher tried to defuse the situation.
mistake.why: Calming tension is *defuse*, like removing a bomb's fuse; *diffuse* means spread out.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Faze* means disturb or unsettle someone and is used mostly in the negative (*nothing fazes her*); *phase* is a stage in a process, and as a verb it appears in *phase in* and *phase out*.
entries.usage: They sound identical, so *it didn't phase me* is a frequent written error, even among native speakers. A few dictionaries list *phase* as a variant spelling, but most editors treat it as a misspelling. *Faze* appears almost only in negatives and questions (*didn't faze him*, *does anything faze her?*) and in the adjective *unfazed*.
examples: The crowd's booing didn't **faze** her; she kept singing.
The first **phase** of the renovation, the kitchen, should be done by March.
The city will **phase out** plastic bags over the next two years.

drill.sentence: Two flat tires on the same trip, and he wasn't even {{fazed}}; he just laughed.
drill.hint: fazed or phased? (unsettled, bothered)

mistake.wrong: The bad reviews didn't phase him at all.
mistake.right: The bad reviews didn't faze him at all.
mistake.why: To unsettle someone is *faze*; *phase* means a stage.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: A *rein* is a strap used to control a horse, so it appears in phrases about control (*rein in*, *free rein*); *reign* is a monarch's period of rule, or to rule.
entries.usage: Because *reign* also suggests power, *free reign* and *reign in* are very common written errors; the correct forms are *free rein*, *rein in spending* and *take the reins*. *Reign* is for monarchs and champions and appears in *reign supreme*. The two words sound identical.
examples: The new chef was given free **rein** to redesign the menu.
Queen Victoria's **reign** lasted almost 64 years.
We need to **rein in** our spending before the holidays.

drill.sentence: After the founder retired, his daughter took over the {{reins}} of the family business.
drill.hint: reins or reigns? (control, as with a horse)

mistake.wrong: The new manager was given free reign to hire her own team.
mistake.right: The new manager was given free rein to hire her own team.
mistake.why: The phrase comes from loosening a horse's reins; *reign* means royal rule.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: A *tenet* is a central principle or belief of a theory, movement or group; a *tenant* is a person who rents a home, office or land.
entries.usage: They differ by one sound, TEN-it vs. TEN-unt, so *tenant* is often written by mistake for *tenet* (*a core tenant of*). *Tenet* is formal and appears with *core*, *basic*, *central* and *key*. *Tenant* belongs to housing and property: *tenants' rights*, *the previous tenant*.
examples: A central **tenet** of good design is that users should never feel stupid.
The previous **tenant** left the apartment in terrible shape.
"Never shop hungry" is the main **tenet** of my mom's grocery strategy.

drill.sentence: One basic {{tenet}} of the Marie Kondo method is that you keep only what sparks joy.
drill.hint: tenet or tenant? (core principle)

mistake.wrong: Honesty is a core tenant of our company culture.
mistake.right: Honesty is a core tenet of our company culture.
mistake.why: A principle is a *tenet*; a *tenant* rents property.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Emigrate* means leave your own country to live in another; *immigrate* means come into a new country to live there.
entries.usage: It is the same move seen from two sides: you *emigrate from* the country you leave and *immigrate to* the country you enter. The nouns follow the same logic: an *emigrant* from Ireland was an *immigrant* in Boston. When both countries are named, either verb is fine (*she emigrated from Chile to Canada*).
examples: My grandparents **emigrated** from Poland in 1956.
She **immigrated** to Canada as a nurse and later became a citizen.
Thousands of Irish families **emigrated** during the famine of the 1840s.

drill.sentence: My parents {{immigrated}} to the United States in 1985 and opened a bakery in Houston.
drill.hint: emigrate or immigrate? (focus on the country they moved into)

mistake.wrong: In the 1980s, many young Irish people immigrated to find work abroad.
mistake.right: In the 1980s, many young Irish people emigrated to find work abroad.
mistake.why: Leaving your own country is *emigrate*; *immigrate* describes arriving in a new one.

entries.label: confusable words
entries.meaning: *Ingenious* means very clever and original; *ingenuous* means innocent, open and trusting, sometimes naive; *disingenuous* means insincere, pretending to know less or care more than you really do.
entries.usage: *Ingenious* describes ideas, solutions and inventors; its noun is *ingenuity*, despite the spelling. *Ingenuous* is rare and literary, while *disingenuous* is common in news and arguments as a polite way to call someone dishonest. Note that *disingenuous* is the opposite of *ingenuous*, not of *ingenious*.
examples: The plumber found an **ingenious** way to fix the leak without tearing out the wall.
It's **disingenuous** to say you didn't know about the fee; it was on the first page.
Her **ingenuous** questions about the city made it clear she'd never left her small town.

drill.sentence: He claims he only wants to help, but that's {{disingenuous}}: he'd make a fortune from the deal.
drill.hint: ingenious, ingenuous or disingenuous? (insincere)

mistake.wrong: What an ingenuous idea! I'd never have thought of that.
mistake.right: What an ingenious idea! I'd never have thought of that.
mistake.why: Clever is *ingenious*; *ingenuous* means innocent or naive.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Intense* describes something extreme in strength, feeling or degree (*intense heat*, *an intense person*); *intensive* describes effort or activity that is concentrated and thorough (*an intensive course*, *intensive care*).
entries.usage: *Intense* is about how strong something feels; *intensive* is about how much work or attention is packed into something. *Intensive* also forms compounds: *labor-intensive*, *capital-intensive*, *time-intensive*. Only *intense* describes people (*he's a bit intense*).
examples: The pain was so **intense** that she had to sit down.
I took a four-week **intensive** Spanish course before moving to Madrid.
After the accident, he spent ten days in **intensive** care.

drill.sentence: Restoring old furniture by hand is very labor-{{intensive}}, so it isn't cheap.
drill.hint: intense or intensive? (needing a lot of work)

mistake.wrong: My father is in intense care after his surgery.
mistake.right: My father is in intensive care after his surgery.
mistake.why: The fixed medical term is *intensive care*: care that is concentrated and constant.

entries.label: confusable words
entries.meaning: An *allusion* is an indirect reference to something; an *illusion* is a false perception or impression; a *delusion* is a false belief that someone holds firmly despite clear evidence.
entries.usage: *Allusion* belongs to texts and speech (*an allusion to Shakespeare*; verb *allude*). *Illusion* is about how things appear (*an optical illusion*, *the illusion of control*), and *delusion* is about what someone believes; in medicine it is a symptom (*delusions of grandeur*). *Be under no illusions* means know the hard truth.
examples: The title is an **allusion** to a famous Beatles song.
Mirrors on the wall create the **illusion** of a bigger room.
He's under the **delusion** that he'll be a millionaire by thirty.

drill.sentence: She has {{delusions}} of grandeur: she thinks she'll be running the company within a year.
drill.hint: allusions, illusions or delusions? (firmly held false beliefs)

mistake.wrong: The poem makes an illusion to Greek mythology.
mistake.right: The poem makes an allusion to Greek mythology.
mistake.why: An indirect reference is an *allusion*; an *illusion* is a false perception.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Allude* means mention something indirectly, without naming it clearly (*allude to*); *elude* means escape or avoid someone, or fail to be understood or remembered.
entries.usage: *Allude* always takes *to*, and careful writers keep it for indirect mentions; for a direct mention, *refer to* is better. *Elude* takes a direct object: *elude capture*, *success eluded him*, *the name eludes me*. The adjective *elusive* (hard to find or catch) belongs to *elude*.
examples: She **alluded** to problems at home but didn't say what they were.
The suspect **eluded** police for three weeks before he was caught.
His name **eludes** me, but I know we met at your wedding.

drill.sentence: A championship ring {{eluded}} him for his entire 15-year career.
drill.hint: allude or elude? (escaped him, was never reached)

mistake.wrong: The answer alludes me.
mistake.right: The answer eludes me.
mistake.why: Something you can't grasp *eludes* you; *allude* means refer indirectly and needs *to*.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Perspective* is a noun: a point of view, or the ability to see things in proportion; *prospective* is an adjective meaning expected or likely to become something (*prospective buyers*).
entries.usage: *Perspective* appears in *from my perspective*, *put things in perspective* and *keep perspective*; *prospective* goes before nouns for future people or things: *prospective students*, *employees*, *parents*, *buyers*. The words sound close, so *perspective clients* is a common slip. In medicine and science, a *prospective study* follows people forward in time.
examples: From my **perspective**, the move to Chicago was the best decision we ever made.
We cleaned the whole house before the **prospective** buyers came by.
Losing my job put everything in **perspective**: health and family matter most.

drill.sentence: The college offers campus tours every Saturday for {{prospective}} students and their parents.
drill.hint: perspective or prospective? (future, likely to become)

mistake.wrong: We're meeting three perspective clients this week.
mistake.right: We're meeting three prospective clients this week.
mistake.why: Possible future clients are *prospective*; *perspective* is a noun meaning point of view.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Moral* is about right and wrong (adjective), or the lesson of a story (noun); *morale* is the confidence and enthusiasm of a person or group.
entries.usage: The stress differs: MOR-ul vs. muh-RAL. *Morale* goes with *boost*, *raise*, *hurt* and *low* (*morale is low*); *moral* goes with *duty*, *support* and *the moral of the story*. *Moral support* (being there to encourage someone) is spelled without an *e*.
examples: Losing six games in a row has destroyed the team's **morale**.
The **moral** of the story: never lend money to friends.
I'm going to her audition just for **moral** support.

drill.sentence: A surprise pizza lunch did wonders for office {{morale}} after a brutal week.
drill.hint: moral or morale? (group spirit, confidence)

mistake.wrong: The coach tried to boost the players' moral before the final.
mistake.right: The coach tried to boost the players' morale before the final.
mistake.why: Confidence and team spirit is *morale*; *moral* is about right and wrong.

entries.label: confusable words
entries.meaning: *Adapt* means change to fit a new situation, or change something for a new use; *adopt* means take something on as your own (an idea, a policy, a child); *adept* is an adjective meaning skilled.
entries.usage: Typical patterns: *adapt to* a new country or job, *adapt a novel for the screen*; *adopt* a plan, an approach, a dog or a child; *adept at* + noun or *-ing*. A company *adopts* a policy (takes it on) and may later *adapt* it (change it). *Adept* is stressed on the second syllable, uh-DEPT.
examples: It took our kids about six months to **adapt** to life in Texas.
We **adopted** a three-legged dog from the shelter last spring.
She's remarkably **adept** at calming angry customers.

drill.sentence: The school board voted to {{adopt}} a new math curriculum starting next fall.
drill.hint: adapt, adopt or adept? (take on as its own)

mistake.wrong: It took me a year to adopt to the cold winters.
mistake.right: It took me a year to adapt to the cold winters.
mistake.why: Adjusting to a new situation is *adapt to*; *adopt* means take something on as your own.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Deprecate* means express disapproval of something or, in software, mark a feature as outdated and due for removal; *depreciate* means lose value over time.
entries.usage: Cars, equipment and currencies *depreciate*; in software, functions and APIs are *deprecated*. *Self-deprecating* (making fun of yourself) is far more common than *self-depreciating*, though both appear. *Depreciated API* is a frequent slip in developer writing.
examples: A new car can **depreciate** by about 20 percent in its first year.
His **self-deprecating** humor makes him easy to like.
This function is **deprecated** and will be removed in the next release.

drill.sentence: The yen {{depreciated}} sharply against the dollar, so our trip to Tokyo was suddenly cheaper.
drill.hint: deprecate or depreciate? (lose value)

mistake.wrong: That API has been depreciated, so use the new one.
mistake.right: That API has been deprecated, so use the new one.
mistake.why: Software features that are being phased out are *deprecated*; *depreciate* means lose value.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Incidence* is how often something happens, usually a rate in a population (*the incidence of diabetes*); an *incident* is a single event, often an unpleasant one.
entries.usage: *Incidence* is common in medicine and statistics (*a high incidence of*, *the incidence rate*). It sounds exactly like *incidents*, so writers mix them up; check whether you mean a rate or several events. In epidemiology, *incidence* (new cases over a period) differs from *prevalence* (all existing cases).
examples: Police said the **incident** was not related to the earlier robbery.
Doctors are tracking the **incidence** of flu in nursing homes this winter.
There were two minor **incidents** at the stadium, but no one was hurt.

drill.sentence: The city has seen a lower {{incidence}} of car theft since the new streetlights went in.
drill.hint: incidence or incident? (rate of occurrence)

mistake.wrong: There were several incidence of theft at the gym last month.
mistake.right: There were several incidents of theft at the gym last month.
mistake.why: Single events are *incidents*; *incidence* means a rate.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *All together* means everyone or everything in one place or at the same time; *altogether* means completely, or in total.
entries.usage: Test it: if you can separate the words (*we were all sitting together*), write two words. *Altogether* is one word for *entirely* (*an altogether different problem*, *stop altogether*) and for totals (*$60 altogether*). They sound the same, so the error is in writing.
examples: It's the first time in ten years our family has been **all together** for the holidays.
With tax and tip, dinner came to $84 **altogether**.
After his heart attack, he quit smoking **altogether**.

drill.sentence: On the count of three, let's sing it {{all together}}.
drill.hint: all together or altogether? (everyone at the same time)

mistake.wrong: I'm not all together sure that's a good idea.
mistake.right: I'm not altogether sure that's a good idea.
mistake.why: Meaning *completely*, it is one word, *altogether*.

entries.label: confusable pair
entries.meaning: *Classic* means typical, or of high and lasting quality (*a classic mistake*, *a classic film*); *classical* means relating to ancient Greece and Rome, or to long-established traditional forms, especially *classical music*.
entries.usage: *Classic* is everyday and usually positive (*a classic car*), and *That's classic!* means typical, often in a funny way. *Classical* is more technical: *classical music*, *architecture*, *ballet*, *physics*. Genre names follow their own logic: *classic rock* is a radio format, while *classical guitar* is a style of playing.
examples: Forgetting your passport on the day of the flight is a **classic** travel mistake.
She listens to **classical** music while she studies.
The museum has a whole wing of **classical** sculpture from Greece and Rome.

drill.sentence: Casablanca is a {{classic}} that every movie lover should see at least once.
drill.hint: classic or classical? (of lasting quality)

mistake.wrong: I love classic music, especially Bach.
mistake.right: I love classical music, especially Bach.
mistake.why: The music of Bach, Mozart and Beethoven is *classical music*; *classic* means typical or of lasting quality.

entries.label: confusable words
entries.meaning: *Oppress* means treat a group cruelly and unjustly over a long time; *repress* means hold back feelings, memories or people by force; *suppress* means stop or hide something deliberately (*suppress a protest*, *a cough*, *evidence*).
entries.usage: *Oppress* takes a group as its object and stresses long-term injustice. *Repress* is common in psychology (*repressed anger*, *repressed memories*), often for feelings pushed down without noticing; *suppress* is more active and deliberate (*suppress a yawn*, *suppress evidence*, *appetite suppressant*). Both *repress* and *suppress* can describe crushing protest, but *suppress* is more common for a single event.
examples: I had to **suppress** a laugh when my boss's dog wandered into the meeting.
For years she **repressed** her anger at her father, until it came out in therapy.
The novel follows a family **oppressed** by a cruel landowner in 19th-century Russia.

drill.sentence: The company was fined for trying to {{suppress}} a report about safety problems at the plant.
drill.hint: oppress, repress or suppress? (deliberately hide or stop)

mistake.wrong: The landowner suppressed the farmers for decades, taking most of their harvest.
mistake.right: The landowner oppressed the farmers for decades, taking most of their harvest.
mistake.why: Long-term cruel treatment of a group is *oppress*; *suppress* is for stopping a specific thing.
